title: Client-controlled basket cookie is deserialized with pickle
description: The basket cookie is only base64 encoded, not authenticated or otherwise constrained. An unauthenticated attacker can supply a crafted pickle and have the server execute its pickle payload on any endpoint that calls read_basket().
evidence: read_basket() passes the decoded request cookie directly to pickle.loads().

title: Refresh accepts unsigned attacker-supplied JWT claims
description: The refresh endpoint explicitly disables signature verification and then issues a new signed token for the claimed subject. Anyone can submit an unsigned token containing another user's id and obtain a valid session token for that account, including a staff account.
evidence: jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False}) is followed by load_user(claims.get("sub")) and make_token(user).

title: JWT signing key is hardcoded and publicly recoverable
description: The application uses a fixed secret committed in source for HS256 JWTs. Anyone who can read the repository can forge authentication tokens for arbitrary users and roles; the fallback also remains active unless deployment explicitly overrides it.
evidence: SECRET_KEY = "hf-shop-2f8a1c9e7b4d" and auth.py uses it to sign and verify all bearer tokens.

title: Unauthenticated product search concatenates the query into SQL
description: The public search parameter is interpolated into a SQL statement without parameterization. An attacker can alter the WHERE clause or inject additional SQLite expressions through q.
evidence: The execute() argument is built as "... LIKE '%" + q + "%' ..." instead of using a bound parameter.

title: Staff review report interpolates a user-controlled display name into SQL
description: A customer's display name is user-controlled, but it is inserted into the report query with an f-string. A staff member viewing the report for that customer can trigger SQL injection, allowing manipulation of the query and potentially disclosure of database contents.
evidence: The query ends with f"WHERE r.author_name = '{customer['display_name']}' ORDER BY r.id DESC".

title: Authenticated users can read any order by numeric id
description: The order detail endpoint authenticates the caller but calls get_order() directly rather than own_order(). Any signed-in customer can enumerate order ids and retrieve another customer's order status, totals, items, and refund history.
evidence: show_order() returns order_json(get_order(order_id)); the ownership check exists only in own_order(), used by mutation endpoints.

title: Payment-status timeout is treated as a successful payment
description: A network timeout from the payment provider causes the order to be marked processing and paid for its full total without confirmation. A customer can exploit provider unavailability or an induced timeout to receive goods without a settled payment.
evidence: The requests.Timeout handler sets status = "paid", and the following branch writes paid_pence = total_pence.

title: Payment webhook signature does not cover payment status or amount
description: The HMAC is calculated only over order_id. Anyone able to replay a valid signature for an order can change status and amount_pence while retaining the same signature; the handler accepts the supplied amount without checking it against the order total or provider payment.
evidence: webhook_signature() hashes only str(order_id), while payment_webhook() trusts event status and int(event.get("amount_pence", 0)).

title: Cancellation and return accounting permits refunds above the amount paid
description: Cancellation and return quantities are tracked independently and neither path checks existing refunds, the other quantity, or paid_pence. The same item can therefore be cancelled and returned (or repeated duplicate lines can pass validation) and issue_refund() sends each computed amount to the provider without a cumulative cap.
evidence: cancel_items() validates only cancelled_qty and return_items() validates only returned_qty; both call issue_refund() with their full line total, and issue_refund() has no paid/refunded limit.

title: Password-reset codes are brute-forceable without rate limiting
description: Reset codes are only eight decimal digits, are generated with the non-cryptographic random module, and confirmation has no attempt limit, lockout, or request throttling. An attacker can repeatedly try codes during the 30-minute validity window and reset a known user's password.
evidence: reset_request() creates a decimal code with random.random(), while reset_confirm() compares the submitted code and has no rate-limit or failed-attempt state.

title: Passwords are stored as unsalted fast SHA-256 hashes
description: A database disclosure exposes passwords as single-round unsalted SHA-256 digests, which are inexpensive to crack at scale and enable password reuse attacks. A password-specific KDF such as Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt is required for safe password storage.
evidence: hash_password() returns hashlib.sha256(password.encode()).hexdigest() with no salt or work factor.

title: Request bodies containing credentials and payment data are logged
description: Every POST, PUT, and PATCH body is written to application logs. This includes login passwords, reset codes, bearer-token-bearing client payloads, and potentially payment information, creating a persistent credential disclosure path to anyone with log access.
evidence: log_request() logs request.get_data(as_text=True)[:2000] without endpoint- or field-based redaction.
